# Three audiences in 2020

## Government

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- $R_t$, the reproduction number over time. How many people each case
  goes on to infect
- Weekly $R_t$, short-term forecasts and ad hoc reports to SPI-M-O, the
  UK government's modelling advisory group, and through it to SAGE, the
  scientific advisory group in an emergency
- What the public saw was a consensus statement on GOV.UK. No team named

> We don't know whether any of this gave any policy maker any useful
> information that helped them make better decisions.
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/comms-shot-spimo-statement.png){width="88%"
fig-align="center"
fig-alt="GOV.UK page: SPI-M-O consensus statement, 17 September 2020"}

::: {.attribution}
[SPI-M-O consensus statement, 17 September 2020](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/spi-m-o-consensus-statement-on-covid-19-17-september-2020),

quote from

## What the consensus process did

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Each group sent its own estimate, with its own model and its own
  interval
- One range went out, agreed by the group
- The shared view survives. The detail behind each estimate does not

> If results are presented individually this can get lost and it
> incentivises being first out (and maybe therefore cutting corners).
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/comms-uk-rt-dashboard.png){height="700px"
fig-align="center"
fig-alt="GOV.UK: latest R range for England, 1.0 to 1.2, no point estimate"}

## The public

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- [epiforecasts.io/covid](https://epiforecasts.io/covid/), April 2020 to
  March 2022
- Daily $R_t$ and nowcasts for several thousand locations. A nowcast is an
  estimate of what has already happened but not yet been reported
- Just over 500,000 unique users and 1.2 million page views by March 2022
- 20,000 of those page views were for the methods page
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/comms-shot-covid-uk.png){width="100%"

## What went wrong

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
> Because we did not have the capacity to manually inspect the data and
> estimates on a daily basis we sometimes published nonsensical estimates.

- Wisconsin reported on a Sunday for the first time. The model read the
  catch-up as an outbreak
- What I wrote down afterwards. Be as open as possible. State the
  limitations first. No point estimates
- I did not talk to the press. No training, no time, and it is someone
  else's speciality
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/comms-shot-covid-issue-171.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="GitHub issue: Your Wisconsin data looks horribly flawed"}

::: {.attribution}
[epiforecasts/covid#171](https://github.com/epiforecasts/covid/issues/171),

:::

## Other scientists

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Forecast hubs. Each team submits weekly and the hub combines them into
  an ensemble
- We submitted to the US, European and German and Polish hubs
- The ensemble beat most single models in most countries
- It also missed the turns the teams missed

> Your forecast becomes part of another product, the forecast ensemble.
> However, they can be very hard to learn from.
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/comms-hub-ensemble-good.png){height="400px"
fig-align="center"
fig-alt="Relative WIS by country, ensemble marked as an asterisk"}

![](../figures/comms-hub-ensemble-less-good.png){height="330px"

fig-alt="Ensemble forecasts for Germany missing the Delta and Omicron turns"}
